retail_intro: Friday's crowd story is conviction under fire: Palantir's margin warning [[n0941]] and Charlie Munger's verdict that retail trading apps are creating a speculative mess [[n1869]] landed on the crowd's favourite tickers the same day war fear returned, the moment when a belief-driven shareholder base either buys the dip or starts to bleed.

retail.title: Palantir Technologies / PLTR — the growth bill hits the faithful
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Palantir is a stock its holders own as a belief system: the data-software company they expect to become the operating system for big institutions, run by a chief executive whose image is part of the pitch, down to the sponsored Norwegian ski clothes NRKbeta investigated [[n0669]]. On Thursday the faithful got the bill for the commercial push: Reuters reports Palantir margins will take a hit from higher spending [[n0941]], and the stock fell 15.75% to 11.77 USD, 19.49% below its 20-session reference of 14.62 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17). The emotional hook now is loyalty: holders who sat through the slide see 11.77 USD as the cheapest entry they will get, and every red day tests whether that conviction is a thesis or a habit.
What Is Driving It

The catalyst is the oldest trade-off in growth investing, spend now to grow later, and Reuters ties the margin hit directly to the commercial push. And the market is in no mood to wait: Meta has lost its top-10 ranking by market value amid its worst month ever, Bloomberg reports [[n0929]]. The macro tape made it worse. Biden said there is a very high risk of a Russian invasion of Ukraine in the next several days [[n1532]], the US says Russia's claim of a troop withdrawal is false [[n1528]], and Al Jazeera reports US stocks took a hit as the crisis stoked fear [[n0964]]. The S&P 500 fell 2.12% to 4,380.26 index points, the Nasdaq 100 2.96% and the VIX jumped 15.73% to 28.11 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17).
The Social Signal

Palantir's drop was the sharpest on the board in a sell-off concentrated in the crowd's favourite tickers: Affirm fell 12.23%, Shopify 11.63%, SOXL 11.34%, Robinhood Markets 9.33% and ARKK 6.44% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17). With the retail broker itself among the losers, the pattern suggests the selling hit the same kind of account across many names at once. The commentary has turned personal: Charlie Munger says retail trading apps are creating a speculative mess [[n1869]] and, in Business Insider's account, blasts traders and slams crypto [[n0869]], while Bloomberg hosts Themis Trading's Joe Saluzzi on the retail investors' rebellion [[n1885]]. The faithful are being told, loudly, that they are the problem, which for a conviction crowd can harden the resolve to hold.
Historical Analog

The freshest reminder of how hard this market punishes a fallen growth favourite is Meta's slide out of the top ten [[n0929]]. The general mechanism is simple: when a company signals that spending will rise before profits do, the market reprices the waiting period, and stocks most dependent on long-dated cash flows fall hardest. Palantir adds a crowd-specific twist. A shareholder base built on conviction tends to hold through the first drop, which can turn a one-day repricing into a slower bleed as late believers give up one by one. The pattern breaks only when the spending starts showing up as revenue that the market can see.
Smart Money View

The split is stark. Cathie Wood says her innovation stocks are way undervalued and recent fund losses temporary, CNBC reports [[n1889]], buy-the-dip faith in its purest form, even as Bloomberg notes her ARKK fund is a year from its peak and still struggling [[n1868]]. Munger stands at the opposite pole, treating the retail-app boom itself as the excess. Large patient money is choosing selectively rather than abandoning the crowd's platforms: Temasek added stakes in Grab, Robinhood and other consumer-focused companies, the Straits Times reports [[n1862]]. For Palantir, the professional debate is whether the commercial spending buys durable growth or simply dilutes margins for longer than holders can wait.
When the Narrative Breaks

The first line is the close itself: a further leg below 11.77 USD would show the margin warning is still being priced, and the 20-session reference of 14.62 USD is the level the faithful must reclaim to call this a shakeout. The macro trigger is the war. Biden's warning [[n1532]] puts weekend headlines in charge, and the Munich Security Conference, where Reuters says the Ukraine crisis takes centre stage [[n0156]], is the next venue for de-escalation or escalation. Rates are the quieter risk: the 10Y Treasury yield closed at 1.97% (US Treasury, prior close 2022-02-17), and a renewed climb would hit long-duration stories like Palantir first. A second red day in Robinhood, the crowd's own broker, would confirm that selling is spreading across retail accounts rather than staying in one name.

retail.title: Bitcoin / BTC — digital gold fails the war test
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Bitcoin's believers call it digital gold, and Thursday was the test. As shelling by Russian-backed separatists raised tensions in east Ukraine [[n1521]], gold rose 1.63% to 1,902.00 USD/oz while bitcoin fell 7.79% to 40,538.01 USD and ether 7.88% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17; Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2022-02-17). The crowd still has smart-money comfort to point to: Sequoia launched a $500 million fund to invest in crypto tokens, Forbes reports [[n1067]], and Warren Buffett invested $1 billion in a crypto-friendly bank years after calling bitcoin rat poison, Fortune notes [[n0828]].
Where It Breaks

The haven story breaks if bitcoin keeps trading like a tech stock on war days. Coinbase fell 7.71% and MicroStrategy 6.98% on the session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17), the Financial Stability Board warns of emerging risks from crypto-assets to global financial stability [[n1053]], and Yahoo Finance tells how the Big Short DAO bet against the crypto market and won [[n1063]]. A daily close below the 20-session reference of 37,784.33 USD would erase the February rebound entirely.

retail.title: DoorDash / DASH — the pandemic habit that stuck
parts: Why Retail Is Here

If Shopify and Roblox were the pandemic trades that faded, DoorDash is the one the crowd can still believe in. The shares soared after record order numbers, CNBC reports [[n0883]]; the Japan Times headline put the surge at more than 30% [[n0884]], and the regular session closed up 10.69% at 105.03 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17). The WSJ says DoorDash showed competitors what it can eat [[n0881]], and Morningstar says the beat broke a losing streak [[n0882]]. The hook is the habit: once people order dinner from an app, they keep doing it.
Where It Breaks

DoorDash is still 17.16% below its 20-session reference of 126.78 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17), so one quarter has not repaired the drawdown. Growth now depends on new categories, such as express grocery delivery with Albertsons [[n0853]], and on pricing power with restaurant partners, where DoorDash is raising fees for McDonald's outlets that keep drivers waiting, the WSJ reports [[n0472]]. If order growth slows as diners return to restaurants, the habit story becomes a reopening casualty.

retail.title: Walmart / WMT — inflation's favourite cashier
parts: Why Retail Is Here

For the crowd's defensive wing, Walmart is the inflation trade anyone can explain: when prices rise, shoppers go to the biggest discounter. Bloomberg says Walmart has a cart full of reasons to love inflation [[n0970]], Modern Retail says it is gaining grocery market share thanks to continued inflation [[n0971]], and the New York Times reports profits grew as consumers continue to spend [[n0973]]. The stock rose 4.01% to 138.88 USD on a day the S&P 500 fell 2.12% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17), exactly the hiding-place behaviour a nervous crowd wants.
Where It Breaks

The same results carry the warning: Walmart says shoppers are on alert as grocery bills climb, CNBC reports [[n0974]], and a consumer squeezed hard enough cuts volume, not just brands. The stock is still 1.66% below its 20-session reference of 141.22 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-17), so the bid has only begun to repair the past month's decline. If war fear fades and the crowd rushes back into growth, a defensive winner can be sold to fund it; giving back the 4.01% gain in a rebound would show it was a hiding place, not a re-rating.
